9
Further Beyond
•
Many behaviours we would like to align neural networks to are not
invertible, nor fully composable. Modelling them escapes the axioms of
group theory required by the geometric deep learning framework.
•
Lifting the invertibility constraint leads us to monoids; an excellent
starting point for alignment to computer science primitives.
•
Lifting compositionality leads us to groupoids, expressing GDL-
consistent models that behave differently across distinct input orbits.
•
Lifting both at once unleashes the full generality of category theory,
embodied within the categorical deep learning framework.
•
It is not always obvious where relevant structures for applying GDL
(groups, or beyond) would come from. Several relevant techniques exist
to approximate or derive such structure, and we cover many of them here.
Groups, representations and equivariance offer a reliable, well-studied basis
for formalising the constraints of neural network architectures. This has been
observed throughout our book’s Chapters. The aim of the introductory mate-
rial of Part I was to provide a solid foundation in the key concepts necessary to
leverage geometric deep learning principles, whereas Part II presented diverse
case studies to show how powerful this framework truly can be for improv-
ing our understanding of neural network architectures—while avoiding getting
bogged down in details for any particular domain of GDL.
While these parts (hopefully!) accomplish the pedagogical aims we had, we
also acknowledge that we’ve covered virtually every popular architecture in
use for deep learning at the time of writing: from graph neural networks and
large language models, through convolutional and recurrent neural networks,
all the way to exotic-domain models such as spherical CNNs, tensor ﬁeld net-
works, or gauge-equivariant mesh CNNs. Given this breadth, it wouldn’t be
all too unexpected for a newly-minted GDL practitioner to presume there is no
point in studying anything beyond GDL! Yet, generalisations of GDL certainly
exist – groups are, relatively speaking, quite simple mathematical structures
258 Chapter 9
– and thinking outside of the Erlangen Program’s conﬁnes can indeed open
horizons in neural network architectures that our blueprint does not cover.
While keeping in mind this is a highly nascent direction, with many roads
left uncharted, this ﬁnal Chapter aims to provide a useful sketch of a roadmap
to navigate it.
9.1 Why Go Beyond Groups?
At its core, equivariance helps architectures gain generalisation capability;
that is, it guarantees a certain type of generalisation (w.r.t. the actions of a
given symmetry group G) must be respected over all possible model inputs.
The key reason to move beyond groups, then, is when they provide insufﬁcient
ﬂexibility to represent a desirable form of generalisation.
To see where such shortcomings might come from, we draw attention to two
speciﬁc group axioms:
g ∈G ∧h ∈G =⇒ gh ∈G (closure / total compositionality)
g ∈G =⇒ g

–1

These axioms felt natural when we aimed to capture the intuitive constraint
that “symmetries should leave objects unchanged”. However, many types of
generalisation we might care about concern transformations that do fundamen-
tally alter the objects they act on, sometimes irreversibly so! Such capabilities
cannot be characterised using the formalisms of GDL we built up so far.
Example 1: Generalising across horizons As a simple example, we are
often interested in designing deep learning architectures capable of size gener-
alisation
1
: they should perform consistently well across inputs of a wide range
of input sizes—even ones never seen during training. This is a notorious pain
point for neural networks, given that most of their success stories are obtained
when generalising in-distribution, i.e. when the patterns found in their training
data properly anticipate the ones found at inference time.
A great inspiration for relevant capabilities of this kind comes from learning
robust computer science primitives, such as algorithms and data structures,
from data (Veli
ˇ
ckovi
´
c and Blundell 2021). For the learnt models to behave
robustly here, the target algorithm’s invariants must be preserved within these
models, irrespective of, e.g., the size or generative distribution of the input.
This implies that any training set we have will likely not cover all possible
scenarios encountered in practical inference.
How can we express a meaningful constraint involving the model’s
behaviour across different input lengths? If we want to follow the spirit of
GDL, we need to ﬁnd a collection of transformations (akin to a symmetry

Two immediate options arise for a set of length-altering transformations:
adding elements to the input, or removing them from the input. The latter turns
out much easier to characterise: for any ﬁnite input of n elements, we have

is the ﬁlter operation in functional programming, which removes all elements

Given the above collection of ﬁltering operations, it is then possible to

ant
2

ﬁlter their input or their output, across all possible predicates (see Figure 9.1).
It should be easy to see why the collection of all ﬁlters does not satisfy
the axioms of a group: deleting items from a set is a non-invertible operation!
Clearly, we must go beyond GDL to analyse ﬁlter equivariant functions. On
this, we fully defer to Lewis et al. (2025) where many beautiful properties
of such functions, and an algorithm for reconstructing them from data, are
260 Chapter 9
provided. What is worthy of noting is that, if we know our function is ﬁlter-
equivariant, only a small number of carefully chosen data points are needed to
reconstruct such functions exactly.
Example 2: Graph-bespoke GNNs Throughout all of our discussions of
graph neural network design – be it relating to generic combinatorial graphs
from Chapter 5, or to geometric graphs from Chapter 8 – we had always
assumed that their parametric components (e.g., the message function, ψ, and
the update function, ϕ, from Equation 5.56) were always fully shared across
all (pairs of) nodes, within all of the graphs we have.
While this is an elegant way of representing a broad range of permutation-
equivariant functions on graphs efﬁciently, strictly speaking, there is no need
for every (non-isomorphic) graph to be processed the same way – each graph
emits its own permutation equivariance constraint, after all, and these do not
interact with each other.

Precisely speaking, to transcend this boundary, we might want to allow certain
transformations g to not have deﬁned inverses g
–1

Depending on which of these constraints we choose to drop, we get one of
three possible generalisations of groups (the monoid, the groupoid, and the
category, respectively)—each with its own set of situations where they might
be particularly useful. They relate to each other by generality as follows:
monoid category

We have already hinted at examples of two of these structures: the collection
of ﬁlter operations forms a monoid, whereas the collection of typed permu-
tations forms a groupoid. It is, of course, possible to drop both conditions,
leading to the general notion
3
of a category. Category theory represents one of
the pinnacles of abstract mathematics, which allowed mathematicians to con-
nect many seemingly disparate results across ﬁelds, due to them having similar
compositional structures—and it is not unexpected that similar efforts are now
inﬂuencing deep learning
4
as well (Gavranovi
´
c 2024).
One important issue that arises when migrating from groups into these less
constrained objects is that it becomes harder to resolve the induced constraints
(as the space of possible solutions grows). Hence, to illustrate the breadth
of possible approaches, we present speciﬁc examples where the derivations
yielded a new kind of architecture. In all cases, there will still be residual ambi-
guity where it is unclear that we chose the best possible class of solutions; we
will clearly indicate these moments in what follows.
9.2.1 Monoids: asynchrony invariance
The ﬁrst object we focus on is the monoid—a “group without inverses”.
Monoids are a great abstraction to study computational primitives, as there
exist exact correspondences between monoid actions and state machines.
As such, it is only ﬁtting that we now elaborate on the asynchrony-invariant
GNN of Dudzik et al. (2024) we hinted at in Chapter 5. As a quick reminder
on motivation: while GNNs are typically implemented fully synchronously
(all nodes transmit and receive messages in parallel, simultaneously), many
computations one might want to do over a graph do not require all nodes to
Further Beyond 263
transmit messages at the same time; a certain degree of asynchrony in the exe-
cution might be preferred. With asynchrony invariance, we instead elect to
keep the model fully synchronous for scalability reasons, but design its com-
ponents such that the ﬁnal embeddings and predictions are the same as if the
messages are being received, and potentially sent, out of sync with each other.
The message, state and argument monoids The forward pass of a GNN
from Chapter 5 (Equation 5.56) exchanges information at varying stages—
to allow us to reason about the order of computation execution, we need to
formalise each of these stages as a separate collection (even though, in practice,
they are all usually latent embeddings in R
k
). In particular, we model different
stages of data processing as the following sets:
•
The messages, M, formalising information sent across an edge.
•
The node state, S, iteratively updated as messages arrive.
•
The node arguments, A, which govern the inputs each node provides to the
message function, ψ.
We further assume a simple but important caveat: both messages and argu-
ments can be iteratively assembled, allowing them a monoid structure. Follow-
ing the usual monoid notation as a triplet of (set of values, binary operation,
identity element), we can write these two monoids as (M, ·, 1) and (A, +, 0),
respectively. Note that the identity elements, or the operation, do not have to be
distinct at all across these two monoids. (The eager reader might wonder why
arguments, A, are important to explicitly track in this way, as in most practical
GNNs, what goes into the message function is the node state, i.e., S = A. Treat-
ing arguments separately will prove critical when reasoning about invariance
to out-of-order message creation and sending.)
Monoid actions and cocycles We can formalise the effect that an incoming
message, m ∈M, has on the state, s ∈S, as follows:
(m, s) 7→(m •s, δ

The ﬁrst row of constraints concerns the interaction of identity elements, and
is as one would expect – an identity message must not change its target’s state,
and it must trigger an identity argument. The composition law for • also fol-
lows the expected form quite closely: given two messages, we either update
the state twice, compositionally, or instead, we compose the messages ﬁrst and
then act on the state with the composed resulting message. This represents an
asynchrony invariance constraint, as once it is satisﬁed, the model may either
transform states with incoming messages immediately as they arrive, or it may
wait to aggregate them ﬁrst before transforming—the outcome is guaranteed
to be the same in both cases.

Dudzik et al. (2024) resolve this tension by showing that if we make the

5
that M= S = A and ⊕= ⊗, we can drop the strict iden-

ϕ(ϕ(x, m), m) = ϕ(x, m) (9.169)
Once we remove the bottleneck on ψ, nothing stops a node from repeatedly
sending the same (potentially partially ready) state multiple times, even when
no new information has arrived. Idempotence resolves this issue: it guarantees
that re-emitting existing states or receiving duplicate messages will not affect
the end result, rendering the strict identity law in Equation 9.167 unnecessary.
One typical way to ensure idempotence, particularly in algorithmic reasoning
research (Veli

Aside: Deep scale spaces As mentioned before, monoids typically arise
when reasoning about computer science constructs, where they serve as a
very neat model of state machines. Further, cocycle conditions on them (a
more generic form of equivariance!) are naturally well-geared towards mod-
elling discrete computational phenomena. However, the ideas discussed in this
subsection can and do ﬁnd application in more perceptual, multimodal input
processing, when dealing with slightly more lossy operations is helpful.
A great example of this are deep scale spaces: image models incorpo-
rating “equivariance” to scaling and coarsening actions (“zooming in/out”)
from Worrall and Welling (2019). In a naïve continuous world, rescaling an
image by a factor s > 0 is a fully invertible operation, and in fact forms a
group. On a discrete pixel grid, however, coarsening an image requires low-
pass ﬁltering (blurring) and subsampling to avoid aliasing. Once ﬁne-grained,
high-frequency details are blurred away, they are irrevocably lost—there is no
inverse operation that can recover them.
Consequently, image coarsening is naturally modelled as a monoid of non-
negative log-scales, ([0, ∞), +, 0). Let S

9.2.2 Groupoids: natural graph networks
Next up, we will discuss the groupoid—a “collection of group-like clus-
ters”. Groupoids can make an excellent abstraction for “typed equivariance”:
enforcing a symmetry constraint across a domain while allowing us to treat cer-
tain collections of input domains differently to each other. Speciﬁcally, input
domains of the same “type” will be processed by the same equivariant model.
As we previously discussed in this Chapter, a particularly neat opportunity
for doing so arises with graph neural networks and permutation equivariance,
as in principle, there is no requirement for two non-isomorphic graphs to be
processed with exactly the same parametric functions. It was de Haan, Cohen,
and Welling (2020) who ﬁrst discovered this opportunity
8
, and realised it
within the natural graph network (NGN) framework, which we discuss next.

Local neighbourhood groupoids, and local NGNs The concept of (global)
natural graph networks (NGNs), built over the adjacency matrix groupoid,
is remarkably powerful. Indeed, it allows us to sharply move away from the
GNNs where every single message function must be the same, while still
being built under the foundational principles of equivariance. However this
proves to be a double-edged sword: when given so much choice, it becomes
computationally intractable to meaningfully take advantage of it in full (with
the exception of speciﬁc problems for which we know the graph structures of
interest well in advance). Furthermore, without signiﬁcant weight sharing, we
strongly risk any ability to generalise outside of the training data distribution.
To make practical NGNs possible, we hence need to move away from global
and into local constraints, as de Haan, Cohen, and Welling (2020) did.
The key insight for local NGNs is simple: rather than conditioning our
model’s message functions on the entire graph’s automorphisms, we focus on
small (e.g., k-hop) local neighbourhoods around that edge. Speciﬁcally, let G

9.2.3 Categorical deep learning
Looking at our journey through this Chapter so far, a curious meta-pattern
emerges. Regardless of which abstraction we used to organise our collection of
transformations – be it groups, monoids or groupoids – the overarching recipe
remained largely the same:
1. Specify our domain
12
and our signal (including in latent spaces);
2. Specify a collection of transformations of interest we want our models to be
“robust” against (group, monoid, groupoid... );
3. Specify how the transformations act on the data domain / signals;
4. Enforce that any neural network layers, f , commute with these actions:

than inventing a bespoke mathematical framework for every transformation
collection of interest, can we capture all symmetry principles – and beyond
– within a single, universal algebraic construct? As established by Gavra-
novi
´
c et al. (2024), the answer is a resounding yes! By stepping up one ﬁnal
level of abstraction into categorical deep learning (CDL), we can reveal that
every constraint we’ve studied so far is a special case of a single concept from
category theory: the monad algebra homomorphism.
We felt strongly that this construction warranted inclusion in this book, and
thought long and hard about how best to present it without simply restating
Further Beyond 279
the formalisms of Gavranovi
´
c et al. (2024). Because a fully rigorous bottom-
up treatment of CDL requires deﬁning a substantial amount of categorical
machinery—lying outside the core focus of this book—we have opted for a
more pedagogical path. Hence, what follows introduces only the minimal cat-
egory theory background needed to build an intuitive grasp of the relevant
concepts and how they map to GDL, in the hope of inspiring interested readers
to explore the foundational literature further.
Group actions as a monad We will build our intuition directly from the
familiar concept of monoid/group actions. Suppose we have a monoid (or
group) of transformations, M, and a feature space, X. Before we even spec-
ify how a transformation m ∈M modiﬁes a vector X ∈X, we can specify
intent to apply this transformation, through pairs (m, X) ∈M×X. This rep-
resents a pending action—an input, X, waiting to be acted upon by m. Within
category theory, this “contained computation” construct around a space, X, is
universally expressed using a monad structure, which we will denote by M(X).
We will not expand on the full formal deﬁnition of a monad in category
theory
14
, and instead opt for a functional programming-aligned exposition, to
keep matters more streamlined. Speciﬁcally, if we follow its signature in lan-
guages such as Haskell, a monad data structure over a space X should support
two kinds of functions, allowing us to manipulate these containers:
•
return : X →M(X)
•
>>= : M(X) →(X →M(Y)) →M(Y)
We can think of return as wrapping an identity computation around X, to cre-
ate a basic monad we can further edit, whereas >>= (also known as “bind”)
allows us to directly operate on the contents of a monad (via its second argu-
ment’s function) as well as potentially composing any wrapped computational
structure through f as well.
Let’s outline how we can represent group actions as monads, as was hinted
previously. We already mentioned that the underlying data structure, M = G ×
–, should be:
•
Monad elements are pairs of a group element and an input signal: (g, X) ∈
M(X), representing “intent to transform X with g”.
•
return X = (e, X); intending to act with the identity creates a “base monad”.
•
To calculate (g, X) >>= f , ﬁrst compute f (X) = (h, Y). Then we can com-
pose:
(

actions are chained and composed through f .

modifying the computational wrapper at all, we can simply combine the
280 Chapter 9
two operators: (g, X) >>= (return ◦f ) will yield (g, f (X)). We will denote this
operation by M(f ) : M(X) →M(Y); in Haskell it is referred to as fmap.
Representations as monad algebra Of course, merely pairing (g, X) ∈
M(X) only allows us to track intended group actions before they’re executed
– it lacks the machinery to perform these actions on our features. We need to
augment our monad with a structure map, a : M(X) →X, which executes its
contained computation. A pair, (X, a), consisting of a space and its structure
map, is then called a monad algebra (or M-algebra), if a respects the monad’s
internal structure:

When M is the previously discussed group action monad M(X) = G ×X,

Armed with monads and their algebras, we can now start to describe neural
networks which might respect the structure in the algebra.
Equivariant layers are monad algebra homomorphisms Now we have a
categorical construction for describing a collection of transformations we care
about (monads) and for explaining how to execute such transformations over a
particular space (algebras).
What are neural networks within this framework? Well, they map between
two spaces: f : X →Y. If f is equivariant to some collection of transformations,
Further Beyond 281
we would expect it to respect the structure of those transformations, across
both of these spaces. Monads, being wrappers over spaces, neatly allow us
to deﬁne both M(X) and M(Y). Algebras, however, are deﬁned with respect
to a space. This means we need to specify separate M-algebras for the input,
(X, a), and the output (Y, b). (Note this is very similar to how we sometimes
needed to represent separate representations ρ
X
and ρ

for input and output
spaces when handling equivariance.)
Of course, f should not be just any mapping between these two spaces—to
qualify as equivariant, it should respect all of the structure contained within
the two algebras. Such a map is called a monad algebra homomorphism, and
it needs to make the following diagram commute:

This is simply stating that, if we have a computation-wrapped input and we’d

while it’s in X space (using the structure map a : M(X) →X) and then call f on
the result, or we can ﬁrst call f on the input, and then execute the computation
on the output in the Y space (using the structure map b : M(Y) →Y).

Beyond symmetry Why did we go through the effort of repackaging the
familiar equivariance condition into the language of monads, algebras and
homomorphisms? The answer is simple: the monad algebra homomorphism
diagram we discovered works for any monad algebra—not only the group
282 Chapter 9
action monad. For example, we can easily swap in monoid actions, or con-
sider monads over families of spaces indexed by groupoid objects, to recover
the other advanced examples studied within this Chapter.
We can also consider examples that go fully beyond what even monoids
or groupoids can express. By swapping out the monad M for other founda-
tional monads in computer science, the exact same homomorphism square
b ◦M(f ) = f ◦a directly transitions into algorithmic and stateful computation.
For instance, choosing M to be the list monad M(X) = X
∗
(which bundles
elements into arbitrary-length sequences) turns M-algebra homomorphisms
into sequence-processing folding operations that underpin recurrent neural
networks (RNNs) and state-space models (SSMs).
Viewed from this perspective, categorical deep learning does not replace the
geometric principles we have studied throughout this book; rather, it reveals
GDL to be the symmetry-pilled branch of a much broader algebraic theory of
neural architectures (Gavranovi
´
c et al. 2024). Whenever we constrain a neural
network to respect the structure of its domain—whether that structure is a 3D
rotation group, a collection of message-processing monoids, a local subgraph
groupoid, or a data structure in theoretical computer science—we are, at the
heart of it, building a monad algebra homomorphism.
9.3 Where Does the Group Come From?
Over the ﬁve years since we ﬁrst released our geometric deep learning proto-
book (Michael M. Bronstein et al. 2021) to the time of writing this ﬁnal
Chapter, we’ve delivered countless lectures, talks and tutorials on the subject.
On virtually every single one of those presentations, one question from the
audience presents itself time and time again: “What if we do not know G?”
This is an important, foundational question about the GDL setup. We side-
stepped it entirely for most of the book by simply assuming the domain, Ω,
the signal space, X, and their symmetry group, G, are known and ﬁxed. Yet,
in many important real-world domains, we may not have easy access to G, or
ﬁnding G might be one of the key scientiﬁc outcomes of the machine learn-
ing system in the ﬁrst place. (The same conclusion, of course, holds for more
general structures than groups that we discussed earlier in this Chapter.)
Rather than viewing this issue as a boundary past which no GDL research
can meaningfully take place, there’s been a vibrant – yet painfully small – fron-
tier of research that tackles this issue head-on from a wide variety of angles. We
opt to use the ﬁnal bit of real estate in our book to survey and credit their efforts,
in the hopes that they serve as a chart for GDL techniques to meaningfully
transition into these “messier” regimes of interest to deep learning.
Further Beyond 283
Direct symmetry discovery from data When the symmetry group acting
on our inputs is unknown, one direct approach to still leveraging it is to explic-
itly parametrise and learn either (a) the generating parameters of the group,
such as basis matrices for Lie algebras (Yang et al. 2023, LieGAN), or (b) data
augmentation distributions that leave the training distribution or task labels
invariant (Benton et al. 2020, Augerino). This allows for learning relevant
group parameters directly from training data, purely through gradient descent.
When we additionally have the beneﬁt of learning over dynamical sys-
tems, we can exploit a physics backdoor coming from one of the heroines
of Chapter 1: Noether’s theorem (Noether 1918). This theorem establishes
a fundamental correspondence between the continuous symmetries of a sys-
tem and its conserved quantities over time (such as energy or momentum).
Inspired by this duality, Alet et al. (2021)’s Noether networks bypass the need
to explicitly parametrise group elements, by instead meta-learning a conserva-
tion law. Given a sequential prediction model f

Making sense of partially observed geometry The previous subsection
focussed on scenarios where symmetries are completely unknown at the onset.
What if, instead, we are fully aware of what G is, but we are fundamentally
unable to observe in full how it acts on our input signal? This is a remarkably
common scenario that arises in most image and video inputs. For example,
we observe a three-dimensional world, on which previously discussed spatial
groups such as SE(3) operate seamlessly. However, making sense of how those
actions map to any 2D projections (e.g. in pictures or video frames) is substan-
tially less trivial due to partial observability of the entire scene at any one point
in time. Earlier works tackled this by explicitly performing SO(3) or SE(3)
actions on latent bottlenecks behind an explicit renderer; see, e.g., Falorsi et
al. (2018) and Dupont et al. (2020). A growing body of recent work attempts
284 Chapter 9
to unearth this unseen geometry, or demonstrate under which conditions it
emerges, within general-purpose 2D neural network backbones.
Leveraging self-supervised learning and interesting inductive biases, Simion
et al. (2026) demonstrate that our understanding of 3D viewpoint symme-
tries can be meaningfully distilled into two-dimensional vision backbones. The
key innovation of their method, 3DPoV, is the emergence of internal symme-
try representations through differentiable sorting and self-supervision. First,
3DPoV extracts keypoints in the input by using an off-the-shelf point track-
ing system (Karaev et al. 2025); then, it explicitly tracks the similarity of the
embeddings of those keypoints against a selection of reference frames. Finally,
self-supervision is performed to enforce that the patch embeddings are equally
ranked by level of correspondence, in both a teacher and a student network.
Ranks are themselves extracted using differentiable sorting, to allow gradients
to propagate through the ranking. Preserving this relative ordering of interme-
diate patch similarities causes an approximately viewpoint-invariant geometric
structure to emerge within a neural network’s representation space: a structure
that is hard to uncover by forcing raw feature vectors to match across severe
changes in perspective.
Taking these ideas a step further, the SeeSE3 framework (C. Chen et
al. 2026) probes whether large, passively trained vision encoders (such as
DINOv2 (Oquab et al. 2024)) spontaneously organise their internal repre-
sentations to mirror the geometry of physical space. While raw differences
between these representations are not directly isomorphic to SE(3), applying a
lightweight Siamese “Poincaré adapter”
15
reveals that relative camera motions
in the Lie algebra se(3) can be linearly decoded from the displacements of
latent features within a neural network. In effect, even when the full extent of
a group’s action is hidden behind a camera lens, sufﬁciently rich multi-view
prediction forces the network’s latent manifold to rediscover SE(3) on its own.
Approximate equivariance Even when we do know the symmetry group, G,
of a domain, Ω, and its effects are fully observable in our signals, X, enforc-
ing its equivariance via strict architectural constraints is not always optimal.
Real-world data frequently exhibits symmetry breaking (in physics, e.g., due
to external ambient force ﬁelds, boundary conditions, or measurement noise),
and the efforts needed to set up an explicitly equivariant model, both in terms of
deriving it and its computational complexity, may not always be warranted—
see Petrache and Trivedi (2023)—especially often when taking into account
the use of (relatively) unrestricted, efﬁcient architectures, such as ones relying
on Transformer backbones.
Further Beyond 285
In Chapter 8 we had already discussed arguably the most striking example
of this: the transition of the AlphaFold model series from leveraging invari-
ant point attention, explicit reference frames and torsion angles (Jumper et
al. 2021), all the way to an approximately equivariant diffusion Transformer
operating directly on raw atomic coordinates (Abramson et al. 2024).
As a transition towards discussing these kinds of models, we start with a
brief overview of elegant ways to retain exact equivariance while decoupling it
from architectural priors (meaning that the model itself can be generic, as the
harness around it guarantees equivariance of the entire system). Such methods
work by either employing a carefully constructed average over a subset of
group-transformed inputs (Puny et al. 2022) or learning a way to represent each
input canonically, so group actions are not needed anymore (Kaba et al. 2023).
When the symmetry itself is only assumed to be approximate, however,
an increasingly popular alternative is to relax it. One might approach this
relaxation architecturally: e.g., by explicitly blending fully-equivariant and
unconstrained layers (Finzi, Benton, and Wilson 2021), or by introducing
insufﬁciently constrained ﬁlter banks in an otherwise equivariant backbone
(Wang, Walters, and Yu 2022). Another option which started gaining traction
recently is to approximate equivariance through the training objective only,
allowing for maximal speedup beneﬁts from generic accelerated foundation
model architectures. Following this route, Elhag et al. (2025) leave the archi-
tectural backbone entirely unconstrained, and instead frame equivariance as
an auxiliary loss term, penalising deviations from the equivariance constraint,

9.4 Closing Remarks
Seeing symmetries relaxed into loss terms, delegated to lightweight canonical-
isation harnesses, or discovered implicitly inside unconstrained Transformers
might tempt the reader to conclude that we never really needed any of this geo-
metric machinery in the ﬁrst place. We argue that the exact opposite is true.
One cannot meaningfully relax, canonicalise, probe for, or regularise towards a
structure without ﬁrst having a rigorous language to deﬁne what that structure
is. Even when a modern architecture chooses to trade strict equivariance for
raw hardware scaling – though even this principle may have caveats (Brehmer
et al. 2025) – geometric deep learning provides the framework to reason about
which inductive biases are being considered, how the data or learning objec-
tive should compensate for any removed ones, and how to measure whether
the model is meaningfully compensating for them within its representations.
And with that realisation, our journey through this book comes full cir-
cle. What began in Chapter 1 as a deep learning adaptation of Felix Klein’s
286 Chapter 9
1872 Erlangen Programme—unifying virtually all of the popular deep learn-
ing architectures in use today through the lens of group equivariance—has
expanded in this ﬁnal Chapter to encompass generalisations to monoids,
groupoids, categories, and even regimes where the symmetry itself may not
be immediately available from raw observations.
Whether a symmetry is hard-wired into a message-passing layer, wrapped
in a monad algebra, hidden in the weights of the neural network itself (as
mentioned in Chapter 3), or loosely injected into a model through data augmen-
tation, a conservation loss, or even fully self-emergent in foundation models,
the foundational lesson of geometric deep learning remains: to understand how
to learn in a complex world, we must ﬁrst understand the structure of what
stays the same.
Suggested Further Reading
Assuming the reader does not have a category theory background already, it is
useful to build a ﬁrmer footing in it; not only to master categorical deep learn-
ing more easily, but also to implicitly help ground monoids and groupoids
better. The more commonly taken route to learning category theory is via
classical pure-mathematics texts. As these often heavily prioritise topological
framings, which are somewhat disconnected from the monad algebra angle we
particularly focus on here, we warmly recommend avoiding these texts at ﬁrst
and starting with resources tailored to computer scientists.
The textbook by Milewski (2019), along with its popular companion video
lecture series, offers an approachable, intuition-ﬁrst introduction to functors,
natural transformations, and monads through the lens of functional program-
ming. For a broader view of how categorical thinking organises compositional
systems across science and engineering, the famous Seven Sketches in Com-
positionality by Fong and Spivak (2019) is an indispensable read. Finally, for
those eager to explore the active intersection of category theory and machine
learning, the comprehensive monograph by Gavranovi
´
c (2024) and the lecture
series, tutorials, and community resources curated by the Categories for AI
(Cats4AI) initiative
16
provide a useful launchpad into this frontier.
